item.title: Six years after TC Yasa in 2020, Naivaka Primary School remains in need of repairs
item.description: Six years after Tropical Cyclone Yasa badly damaged Naivaka Primary School in Bua, the school still has not been fully rehabilitated and remains in need of significant repairs. Education Minister Aseri Radrodro says the school is now among cyclone-affected schools referred to the Ministry of Strategic Planning for rehabilitation.
item.content:encoded:
Six years after Tropical Cyclone Yasa badly damaged Naivaka Primary School in Bua, the school still has not been fully rehabilitated and remains in need of significant repairs.

Education Minister Aseri Radrodro says the school is now among cyclone-affected schools referred to the Ministry of Strategic Planning for rehabilitation.

Radrodro told fijivillage News that the school was initially excluded from the list of schools identified for rehabilitation following an assessment carried out under the previous administration.

He says the Ministry of Education has since taken up the matter and referred the school to the Ministry of Strategic Planning.

Radrodro says the Ministry is also exploring funding from its building grant to assist with the rehabilitation, repairs and maintenance of the school.

He says up to $50,000 could be allocated through the building grant in the current financial year.

Radrodro says the allocation is still being considered, describing the rehabilitation of Naivaka Primary School as a work in progress.

item.title: Pacific Recyclers Alliance call for greater say in decision shaping sector
item.description: Crystal Robanakadavu · 23/08/2026 The Pacific Recyclers Alliance says while it welcomes the growing focus on recycling, environmental policy and investment, grassroots recyclers are still being left out of some discussions that directly affect their work and livelihoods.
item.content:encoded:
Crystal Robanakadavu · 23/08/2026

The Pacific Recyclers Alliance says while it welcomes the growing focus on recycling, environmental policy and investment, grassroots recyclers are still being left out of some discussions that directly affect their work and livelihoods.

Alliance President Amitesh Deo says some organisations have been collecting, sorting and processing recyclable materials for more than 30 years, often with limited formal support.

He says their experience comes from working directly with communities and understanding the realities of recycling in Pacific Island countries, and this knowledge must be considered when shaping future policies and investments.

Deo says recycling should also not focus only on commercially valuable materials, as grassroots organisations deal with low-value and difficult-to-recover materials that still need to be responsibly processed.

The Alliance President says between 2017 and 2026, the Pacific Recycling Foundation, through Waste Recyclers Fiji Limited, recovered 31,874 tonnes of recyclable materials across several waste streams.

PRA Executive Board Member representing Samoa, Marina Keil, says new initiatives and investments should strengthen existing grassroots recycling systems rather than create parallel structures that could weaken them.

The Alliance is calling on governments, development partners, the private sector, academia and civil society to ensure grassroots recyclers are meaningfully involved in designing policies, programmes, investment models and recycling systems.

PRA represents grassroots recycling organisations from Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Solomon Islands, Papua New Guinea, Vanuatu and Nauru.

item.title: Suva Muslim Primary celebrates 100 years of faith, community and legacy
item.description: Meanwhile, Chief Guest and Managing Director of Heavy Duty Industries Shoreeq Azimullah says the school’s future leaders need to ensure young minds are equipped with the skills and tools required to enter the next era. Azimullah also praised the school’s young ambassadors, saying he was impressed by their confidence and efforts throughout the celebrations.
item.content:encoded:
Meanwhile, Chief Guest and Managing Director of Heavy Duty Industries Shoreeq Azimullah says the school’s future leaders need to ensure young minds are equipped with the skills and tools required to enter the next era.

Azimullah also praised the school’s young ambassadors, saying he was impressed by their confidence and efforts throughout the celebrations.

He says their participation is a sign of leadership and an important form of training that cannot simply be taught in a classroom.

He also says every generation faces its own challenges, with technology now advancing at a rapid pace and changing the world on a daily basis.

He says schools need to become more technology-based as the tools of yesterday may not be enough to prepare children for the future.

Azimullah says artificial intelligence will change the job market, with some existing jobs disappearing and new ones being created.

item.title: Fiji’s HIV treatment gap widens as Ministry works to strengthen response
item.description: Fiji is finding people living with HIV faster than it is linking them to treatment and keeping them in care, with only 56 percent of diagnosed people starting treatment in 2025, compared to more than 98 percent in 2021. Minister for Health Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu highlighted this while responding in Parliament to Opposition MP Hem Chand’s question on the progress the Ministry has made towards ac
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is finding people living with HIV faster than it is linking them to treatment and keeping them in care, with only 56 percent of diagnosed people starting treatment in 2025, compared to more than 98 percent in 2021.

Minister for Health Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu highlighted this while responding in Parliament to Opposition MP Hem Chand’s question on the progress the Ministry has made towards achieving Fiji’s target of reducing new HIV infections.

Dr Lalabalavu says closing this gap through same-day treatment starts and active support to keep people in care is the single most powerful action available.

He says the response is being driven through the National HIV Outbreak Response Plan, which the government has established and funded, alongside expanded testing and community-led outreach.

He says Fiji is now in a generalised HIV epidemic.

Insert: Lalabalavu on HIV figures 21st Aug

Dr Lalabalavu says he will not claim that Fiji has already turned the curve downward, adding that the country has not yet reached the turning point, adding that for the first time, the Ministry has a plan and a coordinated response required to bend the curve.

He says there has been measurable progress in identifying people living with HIV adding the number of people who know their HIV status has increased from around 785 in 2022 to about 3,551 in 2025.

He says the number of people on treatment has also increased from about 506 in 2020 to just over 2,000 in 2025.

Dr Lalabalavu says the goal of treatment is to suppress the virus to undetectable levels.

He says a person who is virally suppressed cannot pass HIV, adding that treatment is therefore also prevention as supporting people who start treatment to remain in care and reach viral suppression helps reduce future infections.

He says strengthening viral load testing and the systems behind it forms part of the response plan so the Ministry can be held accountable for this important measure.

The Minister says the Ministry’s own data has identified where the system is failing and the government is acting on it, stressing the Ministry is also focusing on protecting mothers and infants, with women accounting for around 42 percent of new infections.

He says prevention is important in stopping infections before they begin, but the Ministry must also be honest about what is driving the increase.

He says Fiji has also moved quickly to introduce PrEP , or pre-exposure prophylaxis, which is a medicine that an HIV-negative person can take to protect themselves from acquiring HIV.

However, Dr Lalabalavu says uptake has so far been slower than needed because too few people at risk know that the protection exists or how to obtain it.

He says the Ministry is now seeking funding to market PrEP and scale up its use across the country.

Dr Lalabalavu says Fiji is also preferentially accessing Lenacapavir, a breakthrough form of PrEP that requires only two injections a year to provide protection against HIV, adding the first supplies are expected to arrive at the end of this year.

He says a medicine that protects a person for six months at a time has the potential to transform HIV prevention in Fiji, particularly for those who find daily tablets difficult to sustain.
